statement: over 200 survivors found safe, stable housing
subject: The impact of this approach is measurable and meaningful. Last year, our progressive housing model helped over 200 survivors find safe, stable housing while maintaining their autonomy. Our advocacy services supported more than 3,900 individuals as they navigated complex systems and reclaimed their power. To the survivors who trust us, please know we are listening. statement: 123 teens visited Avenue A Teen & Community Center
subject: Avenue A Teen & Community Center - Avenue A continued to offer programming and facilities use to children, teens, and adults of the Monadnock Region. In addition to Friday night teen open hours, the Ave A Club for Great Brook Middle School students (middle schoolers) was created and began in December to provide programming for future teens. Community groups continued to utilize the space, for a donation fee. These groups included Alcoholic Anonymous and the Church of Christ of Antrim. New groups began to use the space for donation as well, which included Al­Anon and a band called Tombstone Territory. Heard It Through The Grapevine Open Mic continued, with 100% of the door and food donations going directly to Avenue A operations. The coordinator of Avenue A Heidi Schultz made many connections with community members, such as Antrim residents, Great Brook Middle School and ConVal High School staff and administration, Monadnock Community Hospital, Antrim Recreation Department, and others who potentially support Avenue A programming. The coordinator participated on Monadnock Community Hospital's Substance Misuse and Behavioral Health Task Force, the HOPE Committee (Antrim's local substance misuse committee) and completed restorative justice training for youth offenders. A generation of teens moved on, and some new faces arrived, with 123 teens and 175 adults visiting the center from July 1, 2014 to June 30, 2015.

statement: 27 families received firewood from the wood bank
subject: Since the community wood bank at The Grapevine began in 2003, we have been pleased to consult with others who have started wood banks over the years in Francestown, Greenfield and Hillsborough, with the most recent wood bank starting up at The River Center in Peterborough.  Free firewood is available for families and individuals who cannot afford to buy wood and who use wood as a primary heat source. statement: as many as 100 people enjoyed community suppers each week

statement: 14 parents and 14 babies participated in Better Beginnings for Babies
subject: Better Beginnings for Babies began its twelfth year. For the third year, parenting educator Nancy Macalaster of Hancock welcomed parents and their infants. Nancy, former family programs director at Sophia's Hearth in Keene, facilitated informal parent discussions and created a nurturing and supportive environment for both parent and baby. 14 parents and 14 babies participated.  Topics discussed included breast and bottle feeding, family bed or crib, sleeping, routines, taking care of yourself so you can care for your baby, balancing work and parenting, parenting styles, crying and other child development issues.

statement: IAVA reached more than 88 million people in 2017
subject: In 2017, IAVA was America's true thought leader, driving the national conversation around veterans, our military, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and the costs and consequences of war. And the numbers speak for themselves: IAVA reached more than 88 million people in 2017. We passed and defended policies in Washington that impacted all 3 million post-9/11 veterans--and our brothers and sisters in the broader national community of 22 million veterans. We connected veterans to peer support through more than 302 VetTogether community-building events across the country. We provided high-touch, in-depth, one-on-one transition assistance to over 900 veterans navigating their returns home, ensuring they got the support that they needed. 1,700 veterans used our online GI Bill Calculator to make the best use of their well-deserved benefits.

subject: The Family Violence Prevention and Services Act, which is part of larger federal legislation, provided funding to develop nationally standardized surveys to help document the work of domestic violence organizations.  The two key survey questions that are used at St. Martha's Hall ask:  As a result of staying in our shelter do you know more ways to plan for your safety and do you know more about community resources? 100% of the women responding said they know more ways to plan for their safety and 95% said they knew more about community resources. 100% of the women stated that they feel more hopeful about the future as a result of their stay. 100% of mothers completing a survey regarding their children stated that they can identify, manage, and appropriately express their emotions and behaviors as a result of their stay.

statement: Louisiana pledged $13.9 million to build an advanced automotive training center
subject: smiley HeiGHTs Following Hurricane Katrina, a new kind of neighborhood called Smiley Heights was proposed by the Foundation. Now overseen by the East Baton Rouge Redevelopment Authority, this innovative plan calls for a blending of homes, offices, retail establishments and generous park spaces-all anchored by educational institutions. In 2012, Smiley Heights made an enormous stride toward becoming a reality when Louisiana pledged $13.9 million to build one of those educational institutions: an advanced automotive training center. Along with the training center, an EBR high school will teach in-demand trades, making Smiley Heights a unique community where education is matched to the workforce needs of growing businesses, helping to ensure good jobs for the people who live there. By 2030, Smiley Heights could ignite the creation of thousands of jobs and revive the surrounding neighborhoods off North Ardenwood and Lobdell. Already, designs for the automotive training center are nearing completion, and construction is expected to begin next year.

The Downtown Development District remade precious green space between the Old State Capitol and the River Center, then announced several additional projects in the works, including a greenway and bike path connecting the city's center with City Park and Memorial Stadium. Meanwhile, the Hampton Inn & Suites was completing construction at year's end, and several new residential projects were unveiled. The Foundation did its part, partnering with the Shaw Center and its tenants to manage a $2.3 million state-funded enhancement of the arts space. Improvements include a new North Boulevard entrance for the Hartley-Vey spaces in the Manship Theatre.

In cooperation with Yelp BR!, Project Purr and Friends of the Animals, CAA has found homes for thousands of adoptable companion animals. The Alliance has set a goal of saving 90% of the animals that come through the doors of the shelter. In light of what they've done already, that goal no longer seems audacious; it is now within reach.

statement: Grants from the Higher Ground Relief fund totaled $3,551,941

Grants from the Higher Ground Relief fund totaled $3,551,941.  The fund bought replacement instruments, helped musicians pay bills and supported performing venues.

statement: The Foundation has granted $1,218,892 to the Greater Baton Rouge Food Bank over the completed decade
